answer_text: Gradient descent is an optimization algorithm used in machine learning to minimize the cost function. It works iteratively, stepping "down the slope" of the function until it finds the minimum. The gradient (the vector of partial derivatives) points in the direction of fastest increase, so the formula has a minus sign in front of it to move in the opposite direction [Source 1].  The learning rate (alpha) sets the step size. If it is too large, the algorithm may overshoot the minimum and never converge. If it is too small, the computation takes very long [Source 2].

In gradient descent, the gradient is a vector of partial derivatives that always points in the direction of the steepest increase of the function. This is why the formula has a minus sign in front of the gradient: we want to move in the opposite direction, downhill, to minimize the cost function [Source 1]. To update the parameters (theta), we subtract the product of alpha (the learning rate) and the gradient from the current theta [Source 3].

If the learning rate (alpha) is set too large, the algorithm can "overshoot" the minimum and never converge. In contrast, a rate that is too small makes the computation take extremely long [Source 2].

Batch gradient descent computes the gradient over the whole dataset, which is slow in practice. SGD (stochastic gradient descent) instead updates the parameters after each individual example. This introduces some noise, but it lets the algorithm escape local minima more quickly [Source 2].

TF-IDF stands for Term Frequency-Inverse Document Frequency. It is a classic technique for turning text into numbers that a computer can understand, and its purpose is to figure out which words actually matter in a document. [Source 1]

IDF is needed because term frequency (TF) alone is not enough. TF only counts how many times a word appears in a text, and common words like "the" or "and" appear everywhere. IDF corrects for this by weighting words according to how rare they are across the collection. It is calculated as the logarithm of the total number of documents divided by the number of documents containing the term, and the log dampens the effect of high-frequency words. Multiplying TF by IDF gives a score in which high values mean the word is both frequent in the document and rare in the rest of the collection. This makes it better than a simple Bag of Words count, which ignores word importance. [Source 1][Source 2]

In the notes, IDF is calculated as the logarithm of the total number of documents divided by the number of documents containing the specific term. The log function matters because it dampens the effect of high-frequency words [Source 2].  For example, with 100 documents and a word that appears in 10 of them, the IDF is log(10) [Source 3].

TF-IDF is better than a simple Bag of Words count because Bag of Words doesn't take word importance into account. Plain counts treat common words like "the" or "and" as significant simply because they appear everywhere. TF-IDF multiplies the term frequency (how often a word appears in a document) by the inverse document frequency (the log of the total number of documents divided by the number of documents containing the term). A high score therefore means the word is frequent in the given document but rare in the rest of the collection, so it highlights the words that actually matter. The log function also dampens the effect of high-frequency words [Source 1][Source 2].

Binary search uses a divide-and-conquer strategy on a sorted array. It looks at the middle element first. If the middle element is the target, the search is done. If the target is smaller, the right half is discarded and the process repeats on the left half. If the target is larger, the search continues on the right half [Source 1].  Because the search space is halved each time, the average and worst-case time complexity is O(log n), compared with O(n) for linear search. The midpoint is best calculated as 'low + (high - low) / 2' to avoid integer overflow [Source 2].  For example, in [1, 3, 5, 7, 9], searching for 7 starts with the middle element, 5. Since 7 > 5, the search moves to the right side [7, 9], where the new middle is 7, so the target is found in two steps [Source 2][Source 3].

The time complexity of binary search is O(log n) for both the average and worst case. This is because the search space is halved at every step. It is much faster than the O(n) time complexity of linear search [Source 2].
It is preferred because it avoids integer overflow issues that can happen in some languages with very large arrays [Source 2].

The tree chooses the split that gives the largest information gain [Source 2]. Entropy is calculated as the sum of probabilities multiplied by their logarithms, with a minus sign [Source 1].

The ReLU (Rectified Linear Unit) activation function is f(x) = max(0, x). If the input is positive, it returns that value. If the input is zero or negative, it returns zero [Source 1].

ReLU is computationally efficient because its formula is very simple, f(x) = max(0, x). It only needs a simple comparison against zero. Sigmoid and Tanh, by contrast, require expensive exponential calculations. [Source 1][Source 3]

The dying ReLU problem occurs when ReLU neurons get stuck at zero and stop learning because their gradient is zero. ReLU's derivative is 1 for positive values and 0 for everything else. For example, if -5 is passed into a ReLU neuron, the output is 0, and if that 0 is passed into another ReLU, the output stays 0 [Source 2].  Leaky ReLU addresses this problem. For negative inputs it uses a small slope alpha, usually 0.01, instead of returning zero. The gradient for negative inputs is then alpha rather than zero, so a neuron with negative inputs can still receive updates and recover, and it never becomes permanently dead [Source 4].
If the input to ReLU is -5, the output is 0. ReLU is defined as f(x) = max(0, x), so any zero or negative input returns zero [Source 1][Source 2].

The core assumption behind the naive Bayes classifier is that attributes are conditionally independent given the class. The joint probability of the attributes given the class is therefore the product of the individual probabilities: P(a_1=v_1, ..., a_n=v_n | c=d) = ∏ P(a_i=v_i | c=d) [Source 1]. Intuitively, the classifier looks at each feature separately and multiplies their contributions, assuming they act independently [Source 2].

**Naive Bayes** - It is a probabilistic classifier based on Bayes' theorem. It classifies objects by computing the posterior probability of each class [Source 1]. - Its key feature is the naive assumption that attributes are independent given the class. The probability of the combined attributes is the product of the individual probabilities P(a_i=v_i | c=d) [Source 1]. - Instead of looking for an identical case, it examines each feature separately and multiplies their contributions [Source 2]. - Typical uses are text classification and predicting a decision to play based on the weather. Zero probabilities are handled with Laplace smoothing [Source 2].  **Decision trees** - They split data into smaller groups by asking questions about specific features. Each split is a node, and the final outcome (a class or value) is a leaf [Source 3]. - Entropy, which measures disorder in the data, is used to decide what to ask first [Source 3]. The split with the greatest Information Gain, meaning the largest drop in entropy, is chosen [Source 4]. - Trees are easy to understand, but they tend to overfit. They are often combined into Random Forests, which build many trees and average or vote over them. A forest is more stable and more resistant to the errors of a single tree [Source 4][Source 5].  **Comparison** - Naive Bayes is probabilistic, multiplies per-feature probabilities, and assumes independence of attributes. A decision tree is a hierarchical model that splits data using entropy and information gain. - The notes mention overfitting and the ensemble remedy (Random Forest) only for trees. A Markov Decision Process (MDP) is the formal mathematical definition underlying reinforcement learning, which aims at long-term maximization of the rewards obtained by an autonomous learner interacting with an unknown environment. It is described as a quadruple consisting of a finite set of states X, a set of actions A, a transition function delta, and a reward function rho [Source 1].  The key feature is the Markov property: transition probabilities and rewards depend only on the current state and the action taken, not on earlier steps in the history. The learner receives no instructions on how to behave, only reward and penalty signals, similar to training an animal or learning to play chess. The task is to find an optimal policy pi: X -> A that maximizes the expected sum of discounted rewards [Source 2].

The Markov property says that transition probabilities and rewards depend only on the current state and the action taken, not on the history of earlier steps [Source 4]. It is a key feature of the Markov Decision Process (MDP), which is the formal mathematical basis of reinforcement learning [Source 3][Source 4].

Q-Learning is off-policy because its update formula assumes the action that maximizes Q in the next state (the max over a of Q(x_t+1, a)). It does not wait for the action the agent actually chooses next under its current policy. Sarsa, by contrast, is on-policy because it uses the action a_t+1 actually selected according to the current strategy [Source 4].  In the Q-Learning update, the target is r_t + gamma * max_a Q_t(x_t+1, a) [Source 2]. This is why Q-Learning learns the optimal path, even though the agent's behavior during learning includes exploratory moves [Source 6].

**Core difference:** Q-Learning is an off-policy algorithm. In its update formula it assumes the action that maximizes Q in the next state. Sarsa is on-policy. It waits for the action a_t+1 that is actually chosen according to the current policy [Source 2].  **Sarsa update:** The name comes from the quintuple (s, a, r, s', a'). The update is Q(s, a) := Q(s, a) + alpha * (r + gamma * Q(s', a') - Q(s, a)). Q-Learning takes the max over actions in the next state, whereas Sarsa takes the value of the action a' that the agent will really choose under its policy, for example epsilon-greedy [Source 3][Source 4].  **Consequence:** Sarsa learns the value of the policy it actually executes, including its random exploratory moves [Source 4].  **Cliff walking example:** Falling off the cliff gives a penalty of -100. - Q-Learning learns the optimal path right at the edge, but often falls during learning because of exploration. - Sarsa learns a safer path farther from the cliff, since it "knows" it will sometimes make a random move [Source 4].  **Results:** During learning, Sarsa usually collects a higher total reward. Q-Learning finds the better final path if exploration is turned off [Source 5].

In Q-Learning, the epsilon-greedy strategy addresses the exploration versus exploitation dilemma. This is the key challenge of balancing trying new actions against using the best-known ones. The Boltzmann (soft-max) rule is another way of solving the same problem [Source 1].

In Adam, the default beta1 is 0.9, which is the decay for the first moment m (the average of gradients). The default beta2 is 0.999, which is the decay for the second moment v (the average of squared gradients) [Source 4].

Adam needs bias correction because its first moment m and second moment v are initialized at zero. At the start of training they are therefore underestimated (biased toward zero). To compensate, they are divided by (1 - beta^t) [Source 5][Source 6].

Leaky ReLU fixes the dying ReLU problem by returning a small slope for negative inputs instead of zero. It is defined as f(x) = x for x > 0 and f(x) = alpha * x for x <= 0, where alpha is usually 0.01. Because the gradient for negative inputs is alpha rather than zero, a neuron with negative inputs can still receive updates and recover, so it never becomes permanently dead. For example, an input of -5 gives -0.05 with alpha = 0.01. [Source 4]  In a standard ReLU, neurons can get stuck at zero and stop learning because their gradient is zero. [Source 2]
With alpha = 0.01, Leaky ReLU returns -0.05 for an input of -5. For negative inputs it computes f(x) = alpha * x, and 0.01 × (-5) = -0.05 [Source 4].

BM25 can be seen as an improved TF-IDF, and two ideas make it better:  1. **Term frequency saturation.** In plain TF-IDF, a word that appears 20 times counts twice as much as one that appears 10 times. In BM25, the contribution of term frequency grows quickly at first and then flattens out. The parameter k1 controls how fast it saturates, with typical values between 1.2 and 2.0. [Source 4][Source 5]  2. **Document length normalization.** A long document naturally contains more words, so BM25 divides by the document length relative to the average document length. The parameter b controls how strong this normalization is. b = 0.75 is the usual default, b = 0 turns it off, and b = 1 applies it fully. [Source 5]  The IDF part is similar to TF-IDF, so rare terms get a higher weight than common ones. [Source 5]

Plain gradient descent has a problem when the cost function looks like a narrow valley: the steps bounce from wall to wall, and progress along the valley is very slow. Momentum fixes this by adding "inertia". Instead of stepping only along the current gradient, it keeps an exponentially weighted average of previous gradients: v = beta * v + gradient. The step is then w = w - lr * v, with a typical beta of 0.9. As a result, oscillations are damped and the step accelerates in a consistent direction [Source 4].
